theme_intro: Depression is one of the most common illnesses in the world, and one of the least understood by the people who have it. This first week lays the ground: what depression is and does, where it comes from, why it is nobody's fault, which myths keep people silent, and what getting help really looks like. Everything that follows builds on one fact: depression is treatable, and most people improve.

days.title: You are not alone, and this is an illness
days.quote: Depression can affect any kind of person at any stage of their life.
days.quote_source: Nathan, Rees, Lim & Correia (2003), Back from the Bluez
days.explanation:
If your mind keeps telling you that something is wrong with you, start here: what you have has a name, and millions of people have it right now.

The World Health Organization estimates that around 300 to 350 million people live with depression. In its World Mental Health Survey across 17 countries, about 1 in 20 adults had been through an episode of depression in the past year alone. Over a lifetime, large population surveys put the figure at roughly 1 in 10 to 1 in 7 people. The Global Burden of Disease study ranked depression second among all causes of years lived with disability in 2019.

Those numbers matter for one reason. Depression is not rare, not strange, and not a sign of weak character. The WHO's own leaflet puts it plainly: it is something that can happen to anybody, and it is not a sign of weakness. It reaches young and old, rich and poor, people of deep faith and people with none.

You did not choose this. Something has gone wrong in the systems that regulate mood, energy and thinking, in the same way that something goes wrong in the body with diabetes or a thyroid problem. That is why it is called an illness, and why, like other illnesses, it responds to treatment and care. This week we will look at what it is, where it comes from and what helps. Today the only task is to let one fact settle: you are one of many, and none of you is to blame.
days.challenge: Today, notice the voice. Each time you catch yourself thinking "What is wrong with me?" or "I ought to be able to cope", answer it, out loud or in your head: "This is depression. It is an illness, and it is common." Do this as often as the voice speaks. Before you sleep, write one line in your journal: how many times did it speak, and how did it feel to answer? If that is too much today, read the sentence above once more and let that be enough.
reflection_questions: When did you first notice that this was more than an ordinary low patch?
Who in your life would you believe if they told you depression was an illness and not a failing? What would they say to you today?
What changes, even slightly, when you call this an illness rather than a weakness?

scripture.text: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.

days.title: What depression does to you
days.quote: Depression slows thinking, impoverishes feelings, and disturbs bodily functions such as sleep and appetite.
days.explanation:
Depression is not one feeling. It is a cluster of changes that touch almost every part of a person, which is why it can be so hard to recognise from the inside. Doctors look for several of these changes lasting two weeks or more and getting in the way of daily life.

Mood is the obvious part: sadness, emptiness, or a flatness where joy used to be. Many people also feel anxious, guilty or worthless. Thinking changes too. The mind turns on itself, dwells on how bad things are, and struggles to concentrate, remember or make even small decisions.

The body is involved. Sleep breaks: waking at four in the morning, or sleeping twelve hours and still feeling exhausted. Appetite falls or climbs. Energy drains away, and sexual interest often disappears. Some people have headaches, stomach trouble or aches that no test explains. The mood often sits heaviest in the morning and lifts a little by evening.

Behaviour shifts last. People stop doing what they used to enjoy, cancel plans, and feel lonely yet unable to reach out. In men and in teenagers depression can look more like irritability or anger than sadness.

Some people also have thoughts of death or of not wanting to be here. These are a symptom of the illness, not a verdict on your life. If you are thinking about ending your life, please call a crisis line today; the Help page has your country's number.

Not everyone has every symptom. Seeing yours written down is the first step towards treating them.
days.challenge: Take a sheet of paper or your journal and draw three columns: Body, Thoughts and feelings, Doing. In each, write the one or two changes you notice most in yourself right now, for example "waking at four", "cannot decide what to eat", "stopped answering messages". Give it ten minutes, no more. This is the same worksheet clinics use; it turns a fog into a list. If that is too much today, write a single word in a single column.
reflection_questions: Which of the changes you wrote down surprised you by being part of depression?
How does your view of yourself, of other people and of the future change when you are depressed?
What would you want someone close to you to understand about what this illness does to your body?

scripture.text: I am weary with my groaning. Every night I flood my bed. I drench my couch with my tears.

days.title: Why it happens: many causes, no fault
days.quote: It is important to understand that depression is not caused by one thing, but probably by a combination of factors interacting with one another.
days.quote_source: Nathan, Rees, Lim & Correia (2003), Back from the Bluez
days.explanation:
When you are depressed, the mind looks for someone to blame and usually settles on you. The research tells a different story: depression grows out of many threads, most of which you never chose.

Some threads are biological. Depression runs in families. In a study that followed three generations for 30 years, children of a depressed parent were about twice as likely to develop major depression themselves. What is inherited is a vulnerability, not a sentence; many people carry it and never become ill. Stress hormones, chemical messengers in the brain, thyroid and other physical illnesses, and the side effects of some common medicines all play a part.

Some threads are life. The loss of a person, a job, your health or a role. An accumulation of pressures: money worries, unemployment, conflict at home, caring for someone, chronic pain. Trauma or neglect early in life can leave the nervous system more sensitive to later threats and disappointments. The WHO lists poverty, loneliness, bereavement and job loss among the strongest risks to mental health.

Some threads are habits of mind: harsh rules about how you ought to be, taking the blame for the bad and none of the credit for the good. These can be unlearned, and next week is about that.

A review of the biology of depression by a Swiss psychiatrist concluded that no single explanation fits everyone; the causes differ from person to person. You did not bring this on by being weak, lazy or faithless. Several threads pulled at once, and the rope gave.
days.challenge: Take five minutes and write the heading "What was pulling on me". Underneath, list anything from the last two years that added weight: a loss, an illness, money pressure, a move, broken sleep, family history, a hard childhood. Do not judge the list or rank it; a fact is enough. Then read it back once and notice how many items you did not choose. If that is too much today, write one item and close the book.
reflection_questions: Which threads in your own story were outside your control?
If a friend showed you the same list, what would you say about whose fault it was?
Is there one thread you would like to understand better this week?

scripture.text: For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.

days.title: The vicious cycle and the small step
days.quote: In depression the brain gets stuck in vicious cycles of negative thoughts and emotions, each feeding the other and leaving little or no room for the positives.
days.explanation:
Depression has a cruel logic. It drains energy and motivation, so you do less. Doing less means fewer moments of pleasure or achievement, so mood sinks further. Undone tasks pile up, and the pile becomes evidence to the mind that you are failing, which drains energy again. Withdrawing from people removes the very contact that could interrupt the spiral. Lying in bed to rest leaves the mind free to replay the same painful thoughts, which clinicians call rumination, and you end up more tired, not less.

The brain also tilts. A depressed mind is sensitised to pick up whatever is negative: a tired face, a grey sky, one unanswered message. Kindness, good food or a sunny morning are noticed less and felt less.

Understanding this is useful, because a cycle can be entered anywhere, so it can be broken anywhere too. The behavioural programmes used in clinics do not wait for motivation to return. They start with action, as small as needed: ten minutes out of bed, five plates washed, the curtains opened. The rule is action first, motivation second. Each small completed step gives the mind a different focus and a small sense of achievement, and over days the cycle begins to turn the other way.

The common mistake is to try too much too soon, fall short, and feel worse. Start smaller than feels reasonable. At first the important thing is not what you do or how much, but that you are doing.
days.challenge: Choose one action that takes under ten minutes and that depression has been stopping: open the curtains and stand in the light for two minutes, wash five dishes, walk to the end of the street, or reply to one message. Name the time you will do it, now. Before and after, rate your mood from 0 to 10 in your journal. If even that is too much, sit up on the edge of the bed for one minute with both feet on the floor. That counts.
reflection_questions: Where does the cycle tend to tighten first for you: doing less, withdrawing, or heavier thoughts?
What did you notice in your mood before and after today's small action?
What is one thing you have stopped doing that you miss?

scripture.text: He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might.

days.title: Myths that keep people silent
days.quote: Depression is a diagnosable condition, not a specific emotion or feeling.
days.explanation:
Many people wait months or years before telling anyone, and much of what silences them is a handful of myths. Here are the worst.

"It is not a real illness; it is sadness or self-pity." Sadness passes; it does not stop you working, sleeping or eating. Depression lasts two weeks or more and changes how you think, feel and act; in a US survey, nearly two thirds of adults who had a depressive episode were severely impaired by it.

"Strong people cope on their own." The World Health Organization says it in plain words: depression is not a sign of weakness. It often reaches the people who have been strong for everyone else.

"Something terrible must have happened." Trauma and loss raise the risk, but depression can arrive when life looks fine from the outside.

"Talking about it makes it worse." The opposite is true. Most people need outside help to get better, and talking therapies are among the best-tested treatments.

"Keep busy and it will pass." Throwing yourself into work rarely helps and often adds exhaustion. Small, chosen activity helps; frantic activity does not.

"Real believers do not get depressed." Two Adventist psychiatrists wrote that believing in God, accepting salvation and being filled with the Spirit do not necessarily spare us from mental pain. Elijah collapsed under a tree in despair. David wrote psalms from the pit. Faith can be a comfort inside depression; it is not a vaccine against it.

Every myth has the same effect: it turns a treatable illness into a private shame. It is neither.
days.challenge: Pick the one myth above that you half believe about yourself. Write it on the left side of a page in your own words, for instance "I ought to be able to manage this alone". On the right, write the fact that answers it, in one sentence. Then read the right-hand side aloud once. Ten minutes at most. If that is too much today, rest your finger on the myth in this message and say, "That one is not true."
reflection_questions: Which myth did you grow up hearing, at home, at work or at church?
Who do you most fear would judge you if they knew? What do you think they actually believe about depression?
What would be different this week if you fully believed the fact on the right side of the page?

scripture.text: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, "Arise and eat!"

days.title: Getting help, and what treatment looks like
days.quote: Depression is a disorder that can be reliably diagnosed and treated in primary care.
days.quote_source: Marcus, Yasamy, van Ommeren, Chisholm & Saxena (2012), WHO
days.explanation:
Most people with depression never receive treatment. In wealthy countries, between a third and a half of people with serious depression had no care in the previous year; worldwide, where figures exist, fewer than half are treated, and in many regions fewer than 30%. Hope is low, energy is low, and the illness itself whispers that nothing would help. So the first thing to know is this: asking for help is not a last resort. It is the expected response to a common medical condition.

Where to start. Your family doctor or local health worker is the right first door. They can rule out physical causes such as thyroid problems or medication side effects, judge how severe the depression is, and either treat you or refer you on. You do not need the right words. "I think I might be depressed" is enough.

What treatment looks like. WHO guidance recommends basic support combined with a talking therapy, antidepressant medication, or both. Cognitive behavioural therapy, interpersonal therapy and problem-solving therapy are brief, structured, and effective for most people who learn their skills. Antidepressants help many people with moderate to severe depression; for mild depression they are not usually the first step, and therapy, self-help and lifestyle matter more. Every decision about medication, including any change, belongs in a conversation with your doctor.

Be patient with the process. Antidepressants usually take two to four weeks to begin working, and therapy builds week by week. Guided self-help, including a programme like this one, works alongside professional care, never in place of it.
days.challenge: Write down the name of one person you could tell: your doctor, a nurse, a pastor, a friend who listens well. Under it, write the first sentence you would say, as plain as "I have not been myself for weeks and I think it might be depression." If you already see a doctor or therapist, write one thing you have not yet told them. If that is too much today, find the phone number of your doctor's practice and save it in your phone. That is the step.
reflection_questions: What has stopped you, or still stops you, from telling a professional how you really are?
If you have had help before, what helped and what did not?
Who would you want beside you, in the waiting room or on the phone, when you take this step?

scripture.text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn't have another to lift him up.

days.title: Depression is treatable: the road ahead
days.quote: Most things in this world are transitory; fortunately, with the right help and support, oftentimes also is depression.
days.explanation:
One symptom of depression is the conviction that it will never end. Abraham Lincoln, in its grip in 1841, wrote that he was "the most miserable man living" and doubted he would ever be better. He was wrong; the illness was speaking. If the thought that it will never end has become a thought of ending your life, please call a crisis line today; the Help page has your country's number.

The WHO puts it in six words: "a solution for depression is at hand". In a trial with 240 low-income women in Chile, 70% of those who received structured, step-by-step care had recovered after six months, compared with 30% on usual care. Trials in Uganda and India found the same with group therapy and lay counsellors. An analysis in The Lancet Psychiatry estimated that widening access to treatment would add 43 million healthy years of life worldwide by 2030.

Honesty matters too. Depression often returns, recovery is rarely a straight line, and many people keep a few residual symptoms for a while. That is why the weeks ahead are not about a quick fix but about building a life that holds you: the thoughts that go round and round, movement, sleep and daylight, food and water, time in nature, loosening alcohol and nicotine, gratitude, connection, faith, and a clear-eyed look at medication. Each has evidence behind it; each works alongside your doctor, never instead.

For today, let the fact stand: most people with depression improve with the right help, and nothing about you rules you out.
days.challenge: Look at the list of the weeks ahead and choose the one area where a small change feels most possible for you right now: thoughts, movement, sleep, food, light, nature, connection or faith. Write it in your journal with one sentence beginning "This week I will try ..." and keep it tiny: a five-minute walk, curtains open at eight, one message to one friend. Then come back tomorrow for day 8. If that is too much today, write only the single word of the area you chose.
reflection_questions: What does "better" look like for you, in one small concrete picture, such as sitting with a coffee and tasting it?
Who or what has helped you through a hard stretch before, even a little?
Which of the coming themes do you feel most hopeful about, and which most wary of?

scripture.text: For his anger is but for a moment. His favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.
